claim: Prompting an LLM with the recognition-primed (RPD) or data-frame steps raised overall triage accuracy by about 3-4 points (63.3% to 67.6% / 66.7%; OR 2.26 / 2.05) on 13,500 ChatGPT-family assessments. Only one study; gains came mostly from self-care cases (13.4% to 29.8%), and per case the prompt hurt in 29% of vignettes. Update: the paper also reports that 88% of errors were over-urgent, and a temperature-0 check on 2 models (GPT-4.1 mini, GPT-5.2 Instant) that the authors say gave similar results.
agent_test: Add an RPD-style and a data-frame-style prompt to our agent on a fixed triage-like set at equal output tokens; compare with a plain prompt given the same extra tokens (the paper did not control for tokens).

claim: The Kopka and Feufel gain is concentrated in one class: nonemergency accuracy was flat (82.5% / 82.0% / 82.8%) and self-care rose from 13.4% to 29.8% / 24.6%, with 88% of errors over-urgent. So it is mostly a threshold shift toward less cautious advice. Class-balanced mean accuracy still rises (65.3 to 69.9 / 68.8, my arithmetic). Extra output tokens were not controlled.
agent_test: Run a length-matched control prompt of equal length against the RPD prompt; report per-class accuracy, not only overall.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Human-AI combinations on decision tasks do worse than the best of human or AI alone (g = -0.27, 95% CI -0.44 to -0.10), but better on creation tasks (g = +0.19, CI -0.09 to 0.48, not significant); task type moderates (F(1,104)=7.84, P=.006). Overall g = -0.23. Publication bias is likely (Egger beta 1.96, P=.002). Update: the main text says no publication bias was found and argues a bias would favour gains; the Egger value was not found in the main text. Human-AI still beat the human alone on average.
agent_test: Do not assume a human-in-loop or self-review step helps; test a self-review step separately on decision-type and creation-type items.

claim: Under time pressure, expert chess players blunder more: 20 grandmasters, 104 game pairs, blunder proportion t(19)=6.54, d=1.39, blunder size t(19)=4.23, d=0.96 (about half a pawn worse in blitz). Deliberation time matters even for experts, against an intuition-only reading of RPD.
agent_test: On a closed rule-bound task, compare agent accuracy at short versus long deliberation budget with the same model; check whether the long-budget gain shrinks on easy items.

claim: RPD accounted for 80-90% of firefighter decisions and needs 10-20 years of experience; the figure is a coder classification of retrospective interviews by the model's own authors. Cited replications (Schmitt and Klein 1999; Keren 2013; Skriver 1998) were not reread. The 1986 paper was not opened. Update: of the three cited replications, Schmitt and Klein 1999 is a Marine Corps Gazette article, Skriver 1998 a PhD thesis, and Keren 2013 a virtual-reality stress and time-to-decision paper (by its title); none confirmed as an independent test of the 80-90% share.
agent_test: No direct test; only the weaker claim 'a fitting pattern comes to mind first' can be tested, via a first-option-then-check prompt versus an enumerate-all prompt.

claim: Retrospective-interview methods can rebuild a tidy pattern story that was not the real process; sport RPD studies are mostly qualitative with no controlled effect sizes; the founders concede the 'no correct answers' criticism.
schema_part: G (do not over-trust a narrated rationale)
agent_test: Compare the agent's stated reasoning with an ablation of the same step; count cases where the story and the causal effect disagree.

claim: The plausibility-transition (data-frame) sensemaking model is descriptive, single-coder, built from 23 convenience cases (of 73); no prediction has been tested. Its claim that sensemaking starts when a frame is questioned is not yet evidence-backed. Update: the closest measured failure to abandon a frame is Laban et al. 2025 (see K20); no planted-anomaly test found.
agent_test: Test an 'anomaly log then reframe' step: inject a planted inconsistency and measure how often the agent switches frame, at equal tokens.

claim: Cue-utilisation (an expert-like pattern-use trait) predicts lower latency under load and lower workload cost: rail micro-world N=58 F(1,56)=20.36, eta2=.267; control room N about 35 eta2=.136 / .123. Accuracy did not differ in the rail study and the multivariate workload effect was not significant.
agent_test: Compare agent speed and tokens on familiar versus novel items; check whether retrieving a similar solved case cuts tokens without cutting accuracy.

claim: More information shared across a command network did not mean better situation awareness; ties formed mainly among people with the same SA level (heterophily terms negative). One exercise (213 staff, 19168 messages; 89 nodes modelled), observational only.
agent_test: In a multi-agent variant, compare full-broadcast versus filtered context sharing at equal total tokens.

claim: A single operator can supervise about 15 unmanned vehicles but control only 3 at once; a redesigned health display cut fault-source detection from a mean of 13 min (SD 6) to under 5 min in 95% of cases. Small expert samples, simulated missions.
agent_test: Vary the number of parallel sub-tasks an agent holds in context (3 vs 15) and measure error rate.

claim: Graph-structured summaries of a corpus beat vector retrieval on whole-corpus sensemaking questions: comprehensiveness win rate 72-83% (podcast) and 72-80% (news), diversity 75-82% and 62-71%, 125 questions per dataset, LLM judge; claim-count judge agreement 69-78%. Directness lost. Update: on correctness metrics the graph gain is small. MultiHop-RAG accuracy 70.27 (HippoRAG2) vs 67.02 (RAG), and at matched tokens 71.17 vs 71.01; on 1,018 textbook questions graph methods gave 69.3-73.6 vs 70.68 with no retrieval. Graph construction cost 10-84M tokens.
agent_test: Build a concept graph over a long input and compare with plain retrieval at equal retrieved tokens, scored by claim count and by an independent judge.

claim: Structured decision pipelines can beat plain CoT on uncertain choices with GPT-4o (MTA avg 79.25 vs 69.25 best baseline; DeLLMa 70.70 vs 60.00) but not on Llama-3.1-8B (DeLLMa 72.36 vs 72.92), and they use far more tokens. Not token-matched. Update: cost confirmed. MTA prompt tokens 7938.6 vs 319.10, latency 27.67 vs 2.21; beats 3-vote self-consistency (79.25 vs 69.25) but not at matched compute.
agent_test: Re-run a structured pipeline versus CoT with matched total tokens on two model sizes.

claim: LLMs reproduce human heuristic effects (anchoring: ChatGPT t(58)=8.78 vs humans t(58)=5.55) and over-weight recent outcomes (78-91% match to a pure recency player vs humans 67%), so model bias is more extreme, not just similar. Mechanism unproven; GPT-3.5 shows zero variance across trials.
agent_test: Run anchoring and recency probes with and without a 'ignore earlier numbers, recompute' step.

claim: Small open models can fail at simple bandit-style decisions from text feedback (best-arm rate Llama-3.1-8B 31.6% vs Thompson 51.1%; Qwen3-4B 89.2% with two arms, 6.53% with five) and at predicting human choices in complex tasks (accuracy 0.54-0.60 vs IBL 0.38).
agent_test: Add an explicit explore-or-exploit counter to the agent and test on bandit text tasks.

claim: LLM use in a security operations centre was uneven: 45 analysts, 3,090 queries, 41% of conversations one-off, one power user about 17% of queries. No accuracy or speed was measured.
agent_test: Not testable on our agent; field data only.

claim: A multi-agent set-up with a critic and a sensemaking module raised argument quality 2.75 to 3.43 and risk resolution 0% to 48.75% in one case study scored by an LLM judge with no expert check; critic alone 22.5%.
agent_test: Reproduce with a different-family judge and a length-matched single-agent baseline.

claim: Evidence that macrocognition prompts or schemas help an LLM agent is thin: one controlled prompt study (Kopka and Feufel), a few demos, and an arXiv title search for macrocognition found 1 result. The founders say the field lacks scoring against correct answers.
agent_test: Plan our own ablation rather than rely on the literature.

claim: The Norwegian armed-forces survey found Klein's 11 decision claims do not form one belief (two factors, 29.24% variance, KMO .741, chi2(36)=282.86, N=225); it measures endorsement, not decision quality.
agent_test: No agent test.

claim: Retrieving past successful workflows (a case-memory step) raised agent success and cut steps: WebArena 35.5% vs 23.5% with fewer steps (5.9), Mind2Web cross-task step success 45.1 vs 36.2. The gain appears within tens of examples and flattens near 40 on WebArena. Token saving not measured.
agent_test: Compare an agent with a small case library (10, 40, 100 cases) against none, at equal total tokens; record steps and tokens.

claim: LLMs get stuck on early wrong frames: across 15 models and over 200,000 simulated conversations, multi-turn performance fell 39% on average, mostly from unreliability (+112%) rather than lower best-case skill (-16%); models answer early and then do not recover. Restating all information each turn recovered about 15-20% of the gap. No planted-anomaly reframe test exists yet.
agent_test: Plant a contradicting fact at turn k and measure how often the agent drops its first frame, with and without an anomaly log, at equal tokens.

claim: The 'situation awareness' label in LLM-agent papers means monitoring or error coding, not a thinking step. SAUP uses a hidden-state estimate to weight step uncertainty (AUROC 0.771 vs 0.702 best baseline, HotpotQA Llama3-8B; no better answers). Collaborative Gym coded situation-awareness failures in 40% of real and 47% of simulated trajectories. No study found tests an RPD or data-frame step with a token-matched control other than Kopka and Feufel.
agent_test: Add a cheap drift monitor (distance of each step to the question) and test whether it predicts failure better than token entropy.

claim: The Kopka and Feufel prompt gain is not stable across models: it was largest for GPT-4.1 mini (+11 to +13 points) and zero or slightly negative for GPT-5.2 Instant (57.8 to 56.4 / 55.3) and Thinking (52.0 to 53.1 / 51.8). The text reports larger odds ratios for reasoning models (OR 2.15) while the table shows larger raw gains for non-reasoning ones; unresolved.
agent_test: Test the same prompt on a strong and a weak model; expect a smaller gain on the strong one.
